title: e2e-latency-profiling-traces-2026-02-20
content:
Purpose:
Capture and summarize end-to-end (E2E) latency profiling traces collected from the serving runtime during the Feb 12-17 load window. Focus is on p50/p95/p99 numbers and per-stage breakdowns to identify bottlenecks and actionable mitigations.

Summary (high-level):
- Testbed: Dedicated GPU pool (A100s, 80GB), 16 vCPU host agents, Linux kernel 6.2, runtime commit abc1234.
- Traffic shape: synthetic mix based on production distribution (short chat queries 60%, medium completions 30%, long synthesis 10%).
- Concurrency targets: low(50 qps), baseline(250 qps), high(800 qps burst).

Overall E2E latency (ms):
- Short requests (<=64 tokens): p50=28 ms, p95=94 ms, p99=210 ms, mean=52 ms
- Medium requests (65-512 tokens): p50=140 ms, p95=420 ms, p99=880 ms, mean=320 ms
- Long requests (>512 tokens): p50=520 ms, p95=1180 ms, p99=2410 ms, mean=980 ms

Observed shape: tail latency increases sharply with sequence length and under high concurrency. Short requests show modest tails driven mostly by queueing; medium/long are dominated by kernel inference and token decode time at the tail.

Per-stage breakdown (p95 median values reported, numbers in ms):
Stages definitions: ingress(network) -> parse -> routing/policy -> queue_wait -> batch_assemble -> kernel_infer -> kv_cache_access -> decode/tokenize -> postprocess -> serialize/egress

Short requests (p95) breakdown:
- ingress: 2 ms
- parse: 1 ms
- routing/policy: 3 ms
- queue_wait: 28 ms (35% of p95)
- batch_assemble: 5 ms
- kernel_infer: 40 ms (47% of p95)
- kv_cache_access: 2 ms
- decode/tokenize: 6 ms
- postprocess: 3 ms
- serialize/egress: 4 ms
Total p95 ~94 ms

Medium requests (p95) breakdown:
- ingress: 3 ms
- parse: 2 ms
- routing/policy: 5 ms
- queue_wait: 60 ms (14% of p95)
- batch_assemble: 12 ms
- kernel_infer: 260 ms (62% of p95)
- kv_cache_access: 18 ms
- decode/tokenize: 30 ms
- postprocess: 10 ms
- serialize/egress: 20 ms
Total p95 ~420 ms

Long requests (p95) breakdown:
- ingress: 4 ms
- parse: 3 ms
- routing/policy: 6 ms
- queue_wait: 120 ms (10% of p95)
- batch_assemble: 30 ms
- kernel_infer: 760 ms (64% of p95)
- kv_cache_access: 80 ms
- decode/tokenize: 100 ms
- postprocess: 30 ms
- serialize/egress: 47 ms
Total p95 ~1180 ms

p99 observations (high-level):
- p99 for short requests driven by extreme queue_wait spikes when autoscaler scales workers (cold-add) and by occasional GC pauses in per-request worker process (we see 160-320 ms spikes).
- p99 for medium/long dominated by kernel_infer path (long-running kernels) and by rare fragmentation in batching that causes single-request batches to fall back to scalar code paths (p99 kernel_infer up to 1.8-2.4x p95).

Trace examples and correlation:
- Trace A (short, p99): long queue_wait (240 ms) followed by normal kernel_infer. Root cause: transient imbalance across worker pool; several workers in drain/scale-down state. Linked trace id: trace-short-2026-02-15-3742 (attached).
- Trace B (medium, p99): kernel_infer holds for 1.6s due to fallback to non-optimized kernel when sequence length exceeded compiled tile size. Root cause: kernel selection mismatch for mid-length sequences. Linked: trace-mid-2026-02-16-4881.
- Trace C (long, p99): heavy KV cache access time (avg 70-120 ms) when cache miss rate spikes due to prefix variation; combined with long decode time. Linked: trace-long-2026-02-17-0034.

Key findings:
1) Kernel inference is the dominant contributor to p95/p99 for medium and long requests (~60-70% of tail). Two sub-causes: suboptimal kernel selection for mid sequences and scalar fallback on fragmentation.
2) Queue_wait is a leading contributor for short-request tails at high concurrency and during scaling events. Transient worker availability and burst scheduling cause 100-300 ms spikes.
3) KV cache misses amplify long-request tails; miss bursts correlate with model-version rollouts and request diversity.
4) Decode/tokenize and post-processing are non-trivial for long outputs (~10-15% of long-request p95) and amplify total E2E time.

Actionable mitigations (short-term):
- Fix kernel selector heuristics to avoid fallback for common mid-sequence lengths (PR exists: https://github.com/redwood-inference/serving-runtime/pull/412). Target: reduce medium p95 kernel_infer by 25-40%.
- Add soft-priority for short requests in routing (local prioritization queue) to reduce queue_wait p95 by ~50% under high concurrency.
- Expand autoscaler warm pool and prefer warm-add over cold-add for burst scaling (reduce cold-add queue spikes).
- Improve KV cache admission policy and add per-customer mini-cache warmup on rollouts to reduce miss storms.
- Instrument per-kernel compile metrics and add histogram export for kernel selection paths to monitoring.

Actionable mitigations (medium-term):
- Investigate quantized kernel paths for mid/long sequences to reduce kernel_infer cost.
- Consider micro-batching affordances that reduce fragmentation at tail (adaptive batch caps by sequence-length class).
- Profile decode/tokenizer hotspots and push decoding into optimized native path (investigate SIMD tokenizer).

Open questions / next steps:
- Need more traces around autoscaler behavior during real production rollout (we have synthetic bursts but not exact rollout traffic).
- Validate kernel selector changes in canary environment with same traffic mix.
- Evaluate trade-offs of prioritization for short requests vs fairness for heavy workloads (SLOs for long-running jobs).
- Collect more p99-level traces with full perf maps (VTUNE / Nsight sampling) for the worst-case kernel_infer events.

Attachments / artifacts:
- Raw trace files (compressed) stored in GDrive folder: /shared_drives/engineering/serving-runtime/traces/2026-02-12_to_02-17.zip
- Grafana dashboard snapshot: https://grafana.redwood-inference.internal/d/latency/e2e-latency-2026-02
- PR: https://github.com/redwood-inference/serving-runtime/pull/412 (kernel selector), https://github.com/redwood-inference/serving-runtime/pull/418 (queue priority)

Owner notes (Liam Chen):
This is an iterative working doc. The kernel selector PR is highest-impact short-term; pairing that with routing priority should give measurable tail improvements for production traffic. Planning to run canary tests next week and capture traces during a controlled rollout. Comments welcome - especially from SRE on autoscaler behavior and from Applied ML on KV cache warmup strategies.
